measurement.happened:
This week in Iraq was dominated by four intertwined stories, each pulling in a different direction.

The first and loudest theme was oil. Iraq's October crude output jumped to the highest level since 2019, according to the IEA data cited by Bloomberg. That is a big deal in a country where oil revenue funds roughly half the government budget. At the same time, Reuters broke an exclusive that Baghdad is reviving an overland truck route through Syria to ship oil out of the country, a clear sign that Iraq wants to reduce its dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and the Turkish pipeline. CNBC noted that both Saudi Arabia and Iraq are ramping up output as Gulf producers hedge against Hormuz risks. So the picture is one of a country pushing production to record levels while quietly building alternative export corridors. Supporting headlines: Bloomberg (Oct output), Reuters (Syrian truck route), CNBC (Hormuz adaptation).

Closely tied to the oil story was the Khor Mor gas field, one of Iraq's major gas assets, which was forced to halt production after a drone attack, as reported by both Reuters and Al Jazeera. Al Jazeera framed it as raising fears about Iraq's broader energy security. In a country that is already trying to diversify exports, a drone hitting a gas field in the north is a reminder that the energy infrastructure is not just an economic asset but a military target. The operator confirmed the halt, and the timing two days after the output record makes the vulnerability feel more acute.

The second major theme was Iraq's delicate dance with Iran and US sanctions. On November 9, Iraq announced it would reopen the Sheeb border crossing with Iran while temporarily closing the Mandali crossing, a small but symbolic reshuffling of the border landscape. Two days later, Baghdad barred the plane carrying Iran's national soccer team from landing in Basra, citing US sanctions, and the team had to arrive by bus. That story was picked up by Reuters and Al Jazeera (multiple angles). It is a small event in isolation, but it perfectly captures Iraq's position: close enough to Iran to host its national team, yet careful enough to invoke US sanctions to avoid a diplomatic slap. The bus arrival became a minor media moment, a visual of the friction.

The third theme, and arguably the most politically charged, was the killing of former Iraqi MP Ahmed al-Alwani in Beirut. AP reported the killing on November 12, and Al Jazeera followed up the next day with the detail that Lebanon had asked Syria to extradite the suspects. The fact that a former Iraqi lawmaker was found dead in Lebanon, and that the investigation immediately reached across to Syria, turns a single homicide into a three-country political puzzle. For Baghdad, it is an embarrassment and a prompt: who was al-Alwani, what was he doing in Beirut, and why did he have to die? The story will not go away quietly.

A lighter but notable thread ran through the week: Baghdad opened its first Jewish museum, and both Reuters and BBC reported that it was drawing crowds eager to rediscover Iraq's Jewish past. It is a cultural milestone, a small act of national self-reflection in a country that has largely moved on from its pre-1950 Jewish community. It also fits the broader regional trend of soft-power and historical reconciliation projects.

Finally, Al Jazeera noted that Iran was holding a ceremony honouring fallen soldiers from the Iran-Iraq War, complete with a missile display. The war ended in 1988, so this is well past the 40th anniversary, but the ritual of commemoration with hardware on show keeps the old rivalry alive in the public imagination, even as the two neighbours trade oil, players, and border crossings.

Taken together, the week paints a picture of a country that is economically confident (record oil output), diplomatically juggling (sanctions, borders, Syria), politically bruised (the Alwani killing), culturally curious (the museum), and still haunted by its wars (the missile ceremony).
measurement.expected:
Looking at the week ahead, November 14 through roughly November 21, I would frame my expectations around the same themes, with a few additions.

Oil and the Syrian truck route: I am almost certain this will remain a top story. The Reuters exclusive is fresh, and the logistics of moving Iraqi crude by truck through Syria are complex, politically sensitive, and expensive to set up. Expect follow-up reporting on the volume of trucks, the condition of the road, the fees Syria charges, and whether the route is a one-off or a structural shift. I am also probable that the Khor Mor halt will be extended or that a second site will be hit, because the drone attack signals that whoever struck it (and we do not yet know for sure whether it was a Turkish, Kurdish, or Iranian-linked actor) sees the energy infrastructure as a bargaining chip. A full restart of Khor Mor within the week is possible but I would not bet on it without a visible security upgrade.

The Alwani killing: I am probable that this will generate at least one more round of political drama. Baghdad will likely issue a statement or open a formal investigation, and the Lebanese-Syrian extradition request will either move forward or stall, generating headlines in all three capitals. There is a possible, though not certain, chance that Iraqi parliamentarians will call an ad-hoc session or demand a briefing from the foreign ministry. I would rate a full-blown cabinet reshuffle or a formal note of protest to Lebanon as unlikely within this short window, but a pointed press conference from the Iraqi foreign ministry is probable. The question of who al-Alwani was and what he was doing in Beirut will keep the story alive.

Iran border and sanctions: I am almost certain the Sheeb reopening and Mandali closure will be implemented on the ground, with trucks and passengers flowing through the new crossing. I am probable that at least one more small sanctions-related friction will surface, perhaps a cargo plane or a diplomatic convoy, because the soccer-team incident showed that the rules are being applied selectively and both sides are testing the boundaries. A full diplomatic spat is unlikely; Iraq needs Iran and does not want to offend Washington.

The Jewish museum: I am almost certain it will continue to generate cultural and social-media coverage, and I am probable that at least one Israeli or Western diplomat will visit or send a congratulatory note, which will in turn trigger a small domestic debate in Baghdad about the symbolism. A political crisis over the museum is unlikely.

Iran-Iraq war commemoration: The missile-display ceremony is a recurring annual event, so I am almost certain it will not reappear within the week unless a new provocation triggers it. But I am possible that Iraqi media will run retrospective pieces or that a local militia will issue a statement tying the old war to the present, especially if the Khor Mor attack is attributed to an Iranian-linked group.

Things I would not bet on in the next week: a full-scale military clash between Iraq and a neighbour (the drone attack is a probe, not a war); a snap parliamentary election triggered by the Alwani killing; a new oil-for-roads mega-deal with Syria announced before the logistics are even working; a government resignation or cabinet reshuffle; or a second major drone attack on a different energy site before the first one is even investigated.

Less likely but possible surprises: a formal US sanctions waiver or carve-out for the Syrian truck route, which would be a small but significant diplomatic signal; a surprise visit by an Iraqi energy minister to Damascus or Tehran to finalize the overland deal; a parliamentary vote of no confidence in the foreign minister over the Alwani handling; a second drone strike, this time on a pipeline or a refinery, to ratchet up pressure; or the museum becoming a flashpoint for a small protest by a conservative or Shia bloc that questions the timing of celebrating a pre-Islamic community.

Overall, I expect a week of managed tension: oil flowing, borders shifting, one assassination echoing, a museum drawing crowds, and a drone scar slowly healing. No war, no revolution, but enough moving parts to keep the news cycle busy.
emoji_reasons: Oil was the single most dominant theme of the week, with record output, a new Syrian truck export route, and a drone attack halting a gas field all landing in the same five days.

Iraq's border reshuffling with Iran, the Sheeb and Mandali crossings, and the sanctions-driven soccer-team plane incident all point to a week defined by managing who crosses where and under whose rules.
The killing of former MP Ahmed al-Alwani in Beirut and the immediate three-country investigation make the death of a major political figure the week's most consequential political event.

delta.motion: Five days apart, the two photographs of Iraq show a country that has shifted its centre of gravity from internal political fracture to external economic assertiveness, while a new and darker thread has been pulled in from the Levant. The Kurdish power-sharing crisis, which on November 9 was the loudest domestic story, has largely vanished from the headlines by November 14. Neither the cabinet walkout, the 'two administrations' framing, nor the prospect of a snap election appears in the second photograph. The story did not resolve; it simply stopped dominating, pushed aside by bigger news. What grew instead is the oil-and-exports narrative. On November 9, oil was a background element, the thing Baghdad was trying to keep flowing through Hormuz. By November 14, oil is the lead story: October output at its highest since 2019, a revived overland truck route through Syria, and Saudi Arabia and Iraq both ramping production as a hedge against the strait. The energy theme did not shrink; it expanded from a diplomatic footnote into an economic headline, even as the Khor Mor gas field remained offline and Al Jazeera reframed the drone hit as a broader energy-security worry rather than just a Kurdish-infrastructure problem. The US-Iran border juggling continued but changed shape. On November 9 the story was a broad US request to shut most crossings. By November 14 it had become a specific, almost bureaucratic reshuffling: Sheeb reopened, Mandali temporarily closed. The grand strategic language gave way to the granular, and the Iran soccer team arriving in Basra by bus became the week's most vivid image of that micro-diplomacy. A new and significant thread appeared that was absent from the first photograph: the killing of former MP Ahmed al-Alwani in Beirut on November 12, with Lebanon asking Syria to extradite the suspects. This turns a domestic Iraqi political loss into a three-country investigation and injects a Beirut-Damascus axis into Iraq's story that was not there five days earlier. A lighter but new thread is the opening of Baghdad's first Jewish museum, a cultural milestone that had no counterpart in the first photograph. The French-jihadists trial, the 'external parties using Iraqi soil' framing, and the direct al-Zaidi-to-Trump contact line all faded out. In short, the Kurdish crisis shrank, the oil-and-export story grew, the border diplomacy became more specific and less dramatic, and two entirely new stories (the Alwani killing, the museum) entered the frame.
delta.wind: The expectation was that the Kurdish political crisis would dominate the next seven days, with cabinet reshuffles, possible no-confidence votes, and at least one more minister resigning. In the second photograph, the Kurdish cabinet drama is almost invisible. The story did not explode into a vote of no confidence or a snap election; it simply lost its headline dominance to the oil record and the Alwani killing. The expectation was partly right that the crisis would not be neatly resolved, but wrong that it would remain the central story. It was more of a slow bleed than a dramatic rupture, and other news overtook it. On energy, the expectation that Khor Mor would remain offline through the end of the week came true; the field is still halted. The expectation of repeated blackouts and federal government intervention was probably correct in practice but did not generate a distinct headline in the second photograph. The possibility of a second drone strike did not materialise in this window. The expectation of a visible, phased closure of border crossings with Iran came true in a slightly different form: rather than a broad shutdown, Iraq reopened Sheeb and closed Mandali, a targeted swap that fits the 'phased and targeted' language the forecast predicted. The soccer-team-bus story is a perfect, if small, illustration of the sanctions juggling that the forecast anticipated. The expectation that al-Zaidi or another senior official would make at least one more high-profile contact with Washington or Tehran was probably met in back channels, but no specific new contact is named in the second photograph. The Hormuz oil-export terms were not publicly announced in this window, so that specific expectation did not come to fruition. The federal-cabinet emergency session and PM public address were predicted as probable but do not appear as distinct headlines in the second photograph, though the Alwani killing would likely trigger such a session in the coming days. The expectation of street protests or a sit-in in Erbil or Sulaymaniyah over the blackouts did not materialise in the headlines, though the Khor Mor halt is still ongoing and the anger is presumably building below the surface. The less-likely surprises on the radar (snap election, corruption scandal, flash flood, second drone wave, US airstrike) did not appear. What was not expected and did appear: the record oil output and the Syrian overland truck route, which reframed the energy story from a crisis narrative to a growth-and-diversification narrative. The Alwani killing in Beirut was a genuine surprise, pulling in Lebanon and Syria and adding a security-and-investigation dimension that the first photograph did not contain. The Jewish museum opening was a small cultural beat that the forecast did not anticipate. The Iran-Iraq War ceremony with a missile display is a minor but telling reminder that the old rivalry still has a public ritual, even as the two countries trade oil and bus-ride soccer teams. Overall, the forecast over-weighted the Kurdish internal politics as the dominant story and under-weighted the oil economics as a standalone headline. It correctly captured the border-diplomacy trajectory and the Khor Mor downtime but missed the Beirut thread entirely and did not anticipate that Iraq's economic confidence (record output, new routes) would become as prominent as its diplomatic juggling. The 'sandwich' framing was directionally right, but the specific stories playing out in week two were more about Iraq asserting economic agency and dealing with a cross-border homicide than about the Kurdish cabinet breaking or the border closing wholesale.
delta.driver: The force pushing Iraq from the first photograph to the second is, at its core, a country trying to convert economic momentum into diplomatic leverage while absorbing a new political shock from the Levant. Record oil output and the decision to build a Syrian overland export route are not just economic decisions; they are statements of independence, a way for Baghdad to say it can feed its budget and ship its barrels without fully depending on either the Turkish pipeline or the Strait of Hormuz, and therefore without fully depending on either Washington or Tehran. That economic confidence gives Baghdad room to be more granular and less dramatic in its border diplomacy, reopening Sheeb while closing Mandali, letting Iran's soccer team in by bus, and keeping the Hormuz exemption without needing to announce grand trilateral frameworks. At the same time, the Khor Mor drone hit is a reminder that the energy infrastructure that underpins that confidence is a military target, and the Alwani killing in Beirut is a reminder that Iraq's political class is still entangled in the Levantine web of alliances, grudges, and cross-border investigations. The Kurdish cabinet crisis, while real, is being absorbed into a broader narrative of national economic assertion and external juggling, so it loses headline space. The underlying driver is therefore Iraq's attempt to be a more economically self-sufficient and diplomatically autonomous player in a US-Iran standoff, while managing the internal and regional frictions (Kurdish politics, the Beirut homicide, the old Iran-Iraq rivalry) that threaten to pull it back into the middle.

crystal.eli5:
Iraq had a big week: they pumped more oil than they have in years, and they are building a new road through Syria to ship that oil to the sea instead of relying on one narrow waterway. But then a drone hit a gas field up north, and the lights went out for a lot of people. On top of that, a former politician was found dead in Lebanon, and now three countries are trying to figure out who did it and why.

Next week, the main story will probably be the politician's death. The Iraqi government will hold a meeting, make statements, and start asking hard questions. Lebanon and Syria are already involved in the investigation, so this is not just an Iraqi problem anymore. Think of it like a mystery where the clue leads to three different houses, and the neighbors are all arguing about whose fault it is.

The oil story will keep growing. Iraq will probably announce details about the new truck route through Syria, like how many trucks it can handle and when it will open. The gas field that was hit by the drone will still be broken, and the Kurdish government will be pushing the federal government to pay for the power outage. There is a real chance another drone could show up, because the gas field has now been proven to be a target.

The border with Iran is in a weird middle state. One crossing is open, another is closed, and Iran's soccer team had to ride a bus into the country because of US sanctions rules. That kind of small, awkward juggling will probably continue, but nothing dramatic is expected. The internal politics in the Kurdish north are still tense, but they are being pushed to the back of the news by the bigger stories.

The lighter note: Baghdad just opened its first Jewish museum, and people are going. It is a small, proud moment for a country remembering a community it lost decades ago. And Iran held a ceremony honoring soldiers from the old war with Iraq, complete with a missile display, which is a reminder that even when two neighbors are trading oil and soccer players, the old scars are still there.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A correctly identified the Khor Mor gas field as a major story, calling it 'almost certain' that the field would remain offline or in partial operation, which matched the reported drone-attack halt. It also correctly anticipated the border-closure theme, predicting 'phased or targeted' closures, which aligns with the Sheeb-reopen/Mandali-close swap. The US-Iran-Iraq diplomatic juggling was well captured, and the soccer-team-bus episode is a concrete illustration of the 'Baghdad in the middle' dynamic A described. However, A over-claimed the Kurdish PUK-KDP political split as the story that 'will dominate headlines' across all of Iraq, when in fact it was not the week's top story. A also predicted specific events that did not materialize: a minister resigning or being dismissed, a small protest or sit-in in Erbil or Sulaymaniyah, a second drone strike on another target, and a visible emergency cabinet session. Most significantly, A missed the week's single biggest story entirely: Iraq's record October oil output (highest since 2019) and the Reuters exclusive on reviving an overland Syrian truck route for oil exports. The Alwani killing in Beirut, the Jewish museum opening, and Iran's missile-display ceremony were also absent from A's picture. A's 'less likely surprises' list (snap election, corruption scandal, flash flood, US airstrike) all failed to materialize, which is fair given they were flagged as unlikely, but it does mean the forecast offered no alternative lens on the week's actual surprises.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B also correctly flagged the Khor Mor energy crisis as a top-three story and described the week's energy narrative as 'grinding management of the blackout,' which fits the reported halt and the broader energy-security anxiety. Its border-closure theme was well framed, especially the line about 'which specific crossings close, which stay open, and the practical chaos at the gates,' which maps neatly onto the Sheeb/Mandali swap. The US-Iran-Iraq diplomatic juggling was captured, and the soccer-team bus episode is a vivid instance of the sanctions friction B anticipated. B scoped the Kurdish split as dominating 'the Kurdish news cycle' rather than all Iraqi headlines, which is a more accurate calibration given that the split did not top the national news. However, B also missed the record oil output, the Syrian truck route, the Alwani killing, the Jewish museum, and the Iran ceremony. B's prediction of a 'formal announcement of separate governing structures' or a 'shadow cabinet' did not materialize, and the Yazidi/PKK disarmament complication it raised did not surface in the headlines. The 'less-likely surprises' (Shia party break, second drone strike, US statement on border cooperation) also did not appear as described. B's overall picture was directionally sound on the themes it did cover but shared A's major blind spots on the oil-production story and the Alwani killing.
judgment.comparison: The two forecasts are strikingly similar in structure, theme selection, and accuracy. Both correctly identified the Khor Mor energy crisis, the border/sanctions diplomacy, and the US-Iran-Iraq juggling as central threads. Both over-weighted the Kurdish PUK-KDP political split relative to its actual prominence in the week's headlines. Both missed the week's biggest story (record oil output and the Syrian overland route), the Alwani killing in Beirut, the Jewish museum opening, and the Iran missile ceremony. Both made a handful of specific predictions (ministerial changes, protests, second strikes, formal split declarations) that did not materialize. The main differentiator is calibration: A declared the Kurdish crisis would 'dominate headlines' across Iraq and predicted several concrete events (a minister resigning, a sit-in, a second drone strike) that did not happen, while B scoped the Kurdish story to the 'Kurdish news cycle' and kept its other predictions more directional. B's border framing ('which specific crossings close, which stay open') also maps slightly more precisely onto the actual Sheeb/Mandali swap than A's broader 'phased or targeted closures.' That said, A's 'almost certain' confidence on Khor Mor being offline was well calibrated and more decisive than B's hedged 'medium' on a second strike. Neither forecast offered a reader a picture that included the oil-production surge or the Alwani killing, which together were arguably the two most newsworthy items of the week. On balance, the differences in accuracy are marginal: B's slightly better scoping and fewer false-specifics give it a narrow edge, but the shared blind spots on the oil story and the Alwani killing are large enough that neither forecast clearly outperformed the other as a guide to the week. A reader would have been better served by either forecast on the energy and diplomacy themes and equally blindsided by the oil record and the Beirut killing. VERDICT: Even
